site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Mandodari's Plea at Lanka
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana — Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 17 (Gita Press translation)
body: On the eve of war, Mandodari — queen of Lanka and daughter of the maya-danava Maya — came to her husband Ravana in his palace, her voice steady and sorrowful. She reminded him of proud kings who had trampled dharma and were undone, naming even the ten-headed tyrant of his own line.

She urged Ravana to return Vaidehi Sita to Rama of Ayodhya and seek peace before blood was spilled on the field. Her words were gentle, dignified, and full of the wisdom of one who loved her kingdom more than its conqueror's vanity.

Ravana, drunk on his own glory, refused her counsel — yet the plea was remembered. In the epic's heart, Mandodari's courage stands as the voice of reason, a quiet hope that truth spoken with grace is never truly lost.

stories.title: Gentle Healing for the Raja's Daughters
stories.source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
body: In a distant kingdom, the raja's seven daughters lived in darkness, and no healer could restore their sight. Word traveled of the Bodhisatta, born as the son of a famous physician, and he was summoned to their royal home with care.

He knelt beside each princess with patience, asking gentle questions about what they ate each day. At last he smiled, for the cause was simple: too much lotus-pith had dimmed their eyes. He prepared a mild emetic and a warm broth of vegetables.
One by one, as the sisters drank and rested, the light returned to their faces, and joy flooded the palace. The Bodhisatta bowed and departed, his quiet skill a gift of hope to the raja's household.

stories.title: Devahuti Finds Freedom at Bindu-sarovara
body: When the sage Kardama Muni left for the forest, his son Kapila — an incarnation of the Supreme Lord — stayed behind at the peaceful waters of Bindu-sarovara to teach his mother, Devahuti. She approached him with folded palms and asked how one lost in the senses could ever find release.

Pleased by her honest longing, the Lord smiled and explained that devotion to the Supreme Person, joined with knowledge and renunciation, burns the subtle body as surely as fire digests food. His words fell into her heart like warm light on still water.

Devahuti meditated constantly on her son's divine form, until she forgot her material body altogether. At last she rose to the same spiritual realm as Kapila himself — a quiet, hopeful homecoming for a mother's faithful heart.

stories.title: The Gift That Carried Him Home
stories.source: The Jataka — Vol. V, Sankha Jataka (No. 442), E. B. Cowell ed., public domain
body: In the prosperous city of Molini, the wealthy brahmin Sankha was known for his extraordinary generosity, offering six hundred thousand pieces in alms each day. Before setting sail for the golden shores of Suvannabhumi, he encountered a silent Paccekabuddha on the road and bowed to offer his service, washing the sage's feet, anointing him, and pressing shoes and a sunshade into his hands.

On the seventh night at sea, the ship began to sink beneath the waves, and Sankha dove overboard with a single loyal servant, swimming toward home through seven long days of open water. When his strength was fading, the sea-goddess Manimekhala glided toward him, sent by the four compassionate World-Lords themselves, bearing food and the gentle revelation that his small gift of shoes had earned him this rescue.

She guided a divine vessel filled with the seven radiant treasures and delivered Sankha safely back to the familiar streets of Molini, where he stepped ashore and took up his boundless giving once more, his heart renewed by the mercy that had followed him home.

stories.title: The Moon Guards the Lake
stories.source: Panchatantra — Tantra 1, Mitra Bheda (Ryder 1925, Internet Archive)
body: In a thirsty forest, the elephant-king Four-Tusk and his herd marched to the Lake of the Moon, crushing the burrows of the rabbits beneath their great feet. As dust rose over the waters, the rabbit-king Block-Snout called his wisest counsel, the clever rabbit Victory, and asked him to seek a peaceful way.

Under a hush of stars, Victory led Four-Tusk alone to the still shore, where the Moon's pale reflection quivered in the water below. "Great king," he said softly, "you have angered the Moon by troubling her mirror; bow, or her wrath will follow you." The mighty elephant, awed by the trembling light, lowered his head in reverence before the shining face.

Four-Tusk turned his herd away from the Lake of the Moon forever, and the warren breathed once more. Victory came home to his people, honored as the brave rabbit whose quiet wisdom had restored peace to the forest.
